scenes.visual: Big navy hook text pops word by word; Norb peeks curious from below.
scenes.cardText: Why does being left out or turned down feel physically painful?
scenes.voiceover: Why does being left out or turned down feel physically painful — like something is actually wrong?

scenes.visual: Left: navy figure with coral spark at foot. Right: phone with coral ✕. Center: mustard brain blob lights up for BOTH.
scenes.voiceover: Your brain has one pain alarm — and it fires for a broken bone the exact same way it fires for being left on read.

scenes.visual: Navy ring wall springs up around a teal creature; reach dots bounce off; creature turns coral.
scenes.voiceover: So your brain treats rejection like a physical threat — and responds by withdrawing, bracing. Which is exactly what keeps you isolated and hurting longer.

scenes.visual: Two creatures slide together; warm pulse blooms; the stressed one calms. Acts out 'connection is pain relief.'
scenes.voiceover: The counter-move is literal: social connection acts like a painkiller. Feeling close to someone dials down the same pain circuit. You are not being soft — you are medicating.

scenes.visual: THE SCIENCE card; painOverlap visual below showing the dual-trigger alarm. Norb curious.
scenes.cardText: Social pain overlap theory: the anterior cingulate cortex registers social exclusion the same way it registers physical injury.
scenes.voiceover: Social pain overlap theory: the anterior cingulate cortex — your brain's pain alarm — registers social exclusion exactly the same way it registers physical injury.

scenes.visual: TRY THIS card; connect visual below. Norb celebrating.
scenes.cardText:
When rejection stings:
reach out to one person you trust — not to vent, just to connect.
scenes.voiceover: When rejection stings, reach out to one person you trust — not to process it, just to connect. That is not weakness. That is neuroscience.
